newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs test NATO's resolve after raid.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs test NATO's resolve after raid.

text.p: Bosnian Serb nationalists, playing on Western reluctance to risk casualties, have launched a low-level retaliation campaign in hopes of forcing NATO to drop a tougher approach towards indicted war criminals, analysts said on Thursday.
A NATO raid against two Serbs wanted for war crimes has sparked a steady stream of threats and minor explosions targeting international monitors and peacekeeping troops over the past week.
No one has been injured in the explosions so far and NATO officers said the incidents did not add up to an organised effort to take revenge on its well-armed troops.
But political analysts said the incidents bore resemblance to Serb attempts in wartime to test the determination of Western powers.

Under the leadership of Radovan Karadzic and army commander General Ratko Mladic, the Serbs managed to stave off sustained NATO bombing for more than three years partly by exploiting fears that military intervention would bring high casualties.
In peacetime, NATO officials had ruled out arresting indicted war crimes suspects, saying such operations could cause casualties and provoke a local backlash against peacekeeping troops.

As it became increasingly clear that indicted war criminals were undermining the peace process, NATO decided to go after two powerful allies of Karadzic. U.S. President Bill Clinton said the operation was ordered to "save" the peace agreement.
The small-scale violence that has followed the raid is testing the nerves and the unity of the alliance.

The United States in particular fears domestic political damage if American soldiers die in a peacekeeping mission that has enjoyed only lukewarm public support. "The Serbs know damn well how this plays at home," said one European diplomat.
Given Washington's fixation with "force protection", it was no coincidence that British soldiers conducted the first arrest operation, the diplomat, who asked not to be named, said.
The Serbs were also trying to exploit long-running divisions among the major powers over how to treat the war crimes issue.

French officials in Sarajevo grumbled that Paris was not properly consulted about last week's raid. French criticism of "Operation Tango" echoed sentiments voiced by Carl Bildt, the former international High Representative to Bosnia, who called it "half-baked".

In a commentary published this week, Bildt said the first arrest operation should have been coordinated with political initiatives and should have targeted the biggest fish indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, Karadzic and Mladic.
The New York Times reported that France had rejected a plan for a snatch operation around Pale, outside Sarajevo, which serves as headquarters for Karadzic and his allies. France denied the report.
Officers in the NATO-led peace force said none of the incidents so far came close to the sort of lethal violence associated with terror campaigns in the Middle East or Northern Ireland.
Yet a sufficient number of shattered windows and publicity was "creating the impression that there was something for the international community to be concerned about," said another Western official.
"The Serbs are playing this brilliantly right now," the official said.

In August 1995, NATO governments decided that military intervention to stop the Bosnian war was worth the risks of possible casualties. Now alliance members are debating whether they are willing to risk the lives of their soldiers to bring war criminals to justice.
